chapters.title: Arrangement of the research
chapters.status: Front matter of the working series
chapters.sentence: The map of the whole series: seventeen answers put into reading order, the rules of evidence every chapter has fixed, and the apparatus of a reference work — concordance, timeline, cases, glossary.
chapters.plain: This document is the map of the whole series. It puts the seventeen answers into reading order, collects the rules of evidence every chapter has fixed, and adds the apparatus of a reference work: a concordance to the nine characteristics of 2014, a master timeline, the cases the series argues from, and a glossary. Read it first, and come back to it whenever a chapter refers to another.

chapters.title: What this research is for
chapters.status: Status: agreed aim, before the historical and pattern chapters
chapters.sentence: This research asks one question — how AI has changed microservice architecture — and answers it under five headings: design, boundaries, communication, operations, and tradeoffs.
chapters.plain: Picture a city. A monolith is one department store: everything under one roof, one set of doors, one power supply. Microservices are a street of small shops, each with its own keys, its own till, and its own opening hours, trading with each other across the street. This research asks a precise question: now that AI helps design, build, and run those shops, did the layout of the street change — or only the tools in the builders’ hands?

chapters.title: Types of software
chapters.status: Four cuts. A program can sit in one cell of each cut at the same time.
chapters.sentence: There is no single list of software types — four cuts answer four different questions, one program sits in one cell of each, and the research question lives on the structure cut.
chapters.plain: Ask ‘what kind of software is this?’ and you get different answers depending on the question behind it: what job does it do beside the hardware; what problem does it solve; how does the customer receive it; how is it structured. A single program sits in one cell of each cut. Keeping the cuts apart stops the research from confusing an AI feature inside an application with an AI tool that redraws the architecture.

chapters.title: The history of microservices
chapters.status: Baseline chapter. This is the architecture AI later meets.
chapters.sentence: Microservices were practiced for a decade before they were named in 2012 and described in 2014 — and that 2014 description is the ruler every later ‘AI changed it’ claim will be measured against.
chapters.plain: Nobody invented microservices on a given day. The habit of small programs that do one thing and talk through simple channels is as old as Unix. Amazon and Netflix practiced it under other names because their single big applications stopped scaling; a group of architects gave it the name in 2012; Lewis and Fowler described it in 2014; and by 2015 the same people were warning about its price. The chapter’s job is to fix the 2014 description as the ruler.

chapters.title: Architectures and design patterns of microservices
chapters.status: Baseline chapter. The pattern language is the before-state for the AI question.
chapters.sentence: Microservice architecture is one style; the patterns are the decisions inside it, arranged as the questions an architect meets in order — and any AI claim must name one of those decisions.
chapters.plain: A pattern is a named, reusable answer to a recurring problem — ‘circuit breaker’, ‘saga’, ‘API gateway’. Richardson’s pattern language is a menu of such answers, arranged as the questions an architect meets in order: where to cut, who owns the data, how a multi-step action survives when one step fails, how services find and talk to each other, how the whole thing stays visible. Read the chapter as a checklist of decisions; the AI question later asks which decisions moved.

chapters.title: Microservice design patterns by the job they do
chapters.status: Full catalog, grouped by the type of problem each pattern serves.
chapters.sentence: Fifteen jobs, sixty-one named patterns, and a Record column that says where every name comes from — this is the row list the whole series refers back to.
chapters.plain: The same menu as the previous chapter, laid out as a table: fifteen jobs, sixty-one named ways of doing them, with a note on where each name comes from — Richardson’s published index, a companion from an older book, or one of the two forms of the saga. It is the row list the rest of the series refers back to, and the maps below draw it in one picture so the shape of the language can be seen before the tables are read.

chapters.title: The patterns in popular software
chapters.status: 61 chapters, one per pattern in the working catalog of Answer 4, in the same 15 parts. Each chapter names the problem, the pattern, the software that shows it, and the cost.
chapters.sentence: Every pattern in the catalog, shown in software people know — chosen on one rule, that the company wrote the decision down — with the problem, the pattern, the named cases, and the cost.
chapters.plain: Every pattern in the catalog, told through software people know: Amazon’s product page, Netflix’s move to the cloud, Uber’s 2,200 services, Airbnb’s migration, Shopify’s decision to stay a monolith, Stripe’s idempotency keys, LinkedIn’s Kafka. Each mini-chapter has the same four beats — the problem, the pattern, the named examples, the cost — so the patterns become stories with a bill attached. Under every chapter heading this edition adds one line in plain words.

chapters.title: Implementing microservices, with domain-driven design as the model
chapters.status: Implementation methods. DDD draws the boundary and the model. Hexagonal architecture, CQRS, and events are how that model is built and connected.
chapters.sentence: A microservice is no smaller than an aggregate and no larger than a bounded context; domain-driven design finds both, and the inside of the service is built so that the business rule lives with the data it governs.
chapters.plain: Domain-driven design (DDD) is a way of thinking about software that starts from the business’s own words. It asks: where does one meaning of ‘order’ or ‘delivery’ end and another begin (a bounded context)? Which cluster of objects must always be consistent together (an aggregate)? The chapter uses a drone-delivery example — a Delivery that a customer may cancel only until a drone has picked it up — and follows one request from the HTTP door to the message that leaves the service, so the reader sees where each rule lives.

chapters.title: Methods that sit beside domain-driven design
chapters.status: The neighbors of DDD: how a team discovers a domain, decides a service cut, builds the inside, connects services, and assigns ownership.
chapters.sentence: DDD has neighbors: workshops that find the domain, forces that decide the cut, drawings that shape the inside, a messaging vocabulary, and methods that assign ownership — and a later claim can name which one an AI tool imitates.
chapters.plain: DDD has neighbours: workshops where business people and engineers map events on a wall (EventStorming), rules of thumb for deciding whether two things should be one service or two (Richardson’s dark energy and dark matter), other ways of drawing the inside of a service (onion, clean, functional core), a shared vocabulary for messages (Enterprise Integration Patterns), and ways of deciding which team owns what (Team Topologies, Data Mesh). None of them replaces DDD; each does a neighbouring job.

chapters.title: How microservices relate to cloud architecture
chapters.status: Cloud architecture is the platform. Microservice architecture is the cut of the application. Cloud native is the overlap.
chapters.sentence: Cloud architecture, cloud native, and microservices are three separate decisions; the cloud did not invent the service boundary — it made the boundary affordable.
chapters.plain: Three different questions get mixed together under the word ‘cloud’. Where does the software run (cloud architecture)? Is it built to use an elastic platform (cloud native)? How is the application divided into services (microservices)? You can answer yes to any one without the others: a monolith can run in the cloud; a microservice suite can run in your own basement. The cloud’s real contribution is that it made many small deployable units affordable.

chapters.title: Kubernetes from the point of view of microservices
chapters.status: Kubernetes keeps instances alive and addressable. The microservice architecture decides what those instances mean.
chapters.sentence: Kubernetes keeps instances alive and addressable; it is not a microservice architecture, and it will happily run a well-cut suite, a monolith, or a distributed monolith without telling them apart.
chapters.plain: Kubernetes is the crew that keeps containers running, replaces them when they die, and gives each group of them a stable name. It knows nothing about orders, deliveries, or business rules. Think of two loops: the platform’s loop asks ‘are three copies running and reachable?’; the domain’s loop asks ‘may this delivery be cancelled?’. The first cannot fix a mistake in the second.

chapters.title: PaaS from the point of view of microservices
chapters.status: PaaS here is Platform as a Service. The spelling Pass in the question is read as that cloud model.
chapters.sentence: A PaaS is the platform a service is pushed to: it runs, routes, restarts, and scales the process, and it neither knows nor cares whether that process is a microservice.
chapters.plain: A PaaS is the platform you hand your code to: ‘here is my app, here are its process types, here is the database I want attached’. Heroku made this a git push. The platform runs, routes, restarts, and scales; it neither knows nor cares whether two apps share a database or whether a message carries a tenant. The service still has to mean something; the platform only keeps it running.

chapters.title: Requirements of a SaaS system
chapters.status: SaaS here is Software as a Service. The spelling SAS in the question is read as that cloud model, not as the SAS analytics product.
chapters.sentence: Software as a service means one product run by the provider for many tenants — so multi-tenancy is the architectural consequence, and every request, message, row, and log line must know its tenant.
chapters.plain: Software as a service means one product, run by the provider, used by many customer organizations (tenants) at once. Multi-tenancy is the consequence: every request must carry which tenant it belongs to, every row must be attributable to a tenant, and the provider needs a control plane — the back office that onboards tenants, meters their use, and applies their tier. Microservices do not change these obligations; they multiply the places where each must be honored.

chapters.title: What sits beside SaaS
chapters.status: NIST names three service models. PaaS and SaaS already have chapters. This chapter adds IaaS and the narrower names the industry hangs on the three.
chapters.sentence: There are exactly three official ‘as a service’ models — infrastructure, platform, software — sorted by who the customer is; every newer name lands under one of them.
chapters.plain: There are exactly three official ‘as a service’ models — infrastructure, platform, software — sorted by who the customer is: an operator, a developer, or an end user. Every newer label (function-, container-, database-, identity-as-a-service, and so on) is a narrower product that still lands under one of the three. And ‘public, private, hybrid’ is a different question altogether: where the cloud runs.

chapters.title: Functional and non-functional requirements
chapters.status: Functional requirements are the behavior. Non-functional requirements are the qualities and constraints on that behavior.
chapters.sentence: Functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional requirements say how well and under what constraints — and services are usually split to satisfy the second kind.
chapters.plain: A functional requirement says what the system does: ‘a customer can cancel a delivery before pickup’. A non-functional requirement says how well, and under what constraints: how fast, how available, how isolated between tenants, in which country the data may live. Both must be testable. Services are usually split to satisfy a non-functional requirement — and regretted when the non-functional cost of splitting was never written down.

chapters.title: Software engineering
chapters.status: The discipline. SWEBOK names the knowledge. ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 names the life-cycle processes.
chapters.sentence: Software engineering is the discipline that produces every product in the series: eighteen knowledge areas, thirty life-cycle processes, and no prescribed life-cycle model — so a tool’s work can be named by the area it practices and what it still owes.
chapters.plain: Software engineering is the discipline that produces every product in the earlier chapters. The SWEBOK Guide names its eighteen areas of knowledge; the ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 standard names the thirty processes of a software life cycle, and refuses to choose a life-cycle model for you. Cancelling a delivery is walked through all fourteen technical processes so the reader can see the work each name stands for — and where a tool’s contribution can be graded.

chapters.title: Design patterns of the AI system
chapters.status: One chapter for each pattern. The names come from two published sources, plus the retrieval paper the augmented model depends on.
chapters.sentence: Inside a service, a language-model call can be arranged in thirteen shapes, from a single call to an autonomous agent — but these are control structures for model calls, and the microservice baseline remains the control structure for business facts.
chapters.plain: Inside a service, a language-model call can be arranged in several shapes: one call, one model with tools, a fixed chain, a router, parallel calls, a model that delegates, a maker and a checker, a group discussion, a hand-off, a manager with a ledger, a free-roaming agent, and a stop for a human. Each shape is placed in the drone-delivery estate and paired with the microservice decision it most resembles — with one recurring warning: the model never becomes the owner of the business fact.

chapters.title: What AI changed
chapters.status: Chapters 17–21 of the reading order, under the five headings of the aim
chapters.sentence: In the cases written down by September 2026, AI changed the architecture of the call to a model. It did not draw the business boundary, own the fact, or accept the change.
chapters.plain: The last part of the series grades real announcements against the rules the earlier chapters fixed. A workshop, not a model, drew QRRA’s six services; the tool wrote the deployment code. Shopify kept one assistant and had to teach its judge not to cheat. Netflix put a smart router on the path to its models, measured the delay and the outage risk, and moved the payload back onto Envoy. Uber and an Envoy gateway put one door in front of model vendors. A coding agent may open a pull request; a person still lets the pipeline run. The new bill is tokens. The old bill — latency, a single point of failure — came back and was paid.
